title: Kenyan Pilau
subtitle: kenyan spiced rice with meat
excerpt: A deeply aromatic one-pot rice dish cooked with chicken, whole spices and stock. Kenyan pilau is richer and more heavily spiced than its South Asian cousins.
sourceNotes: Pilau arrived in East Africa through centuries of Indian Ocean trade. The Kenyan version has evolved a distinct character, using a heavier hand with black pepper and whole spices.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The rice can be cooked 2 hours ahead and kept covered. Reheat gently with a sprinkle of water.

glossaryTerms.definition: A spiced rice dish cooked in stock with meat, common across East Africa and South Asia.

content.text: is built on whole spices fried in oil before anything else goes in. Cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and black peppercorns crack and sizzle in the pan for the first minute. That initial fry is what gives the finished rice its deep, warm fragrance.
Rinse the rice well until the water runs clear. This removes surface starch and keeps the grains separate after cooking.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium-high heat. Add the whole peppercorns and cook for 30 seconds until they start to pop. Add the sliced onion and fry for 10 minutes until deep golden brown.
Add the garlic, ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, allspice, cumin and coriander. Stir for 2 minutes. Add the tomatoes and cook for 3 minutes until soft.
Add the chicken thighs and turn to coat in the spice mixture. Brown for 5 minutes, turning once.
Pour in the hot stock and bring to the boil. Reduce to a simmer and cook uncovered for 15 minutes until the chicken is almost cooked through.

Add the rinsed rice and stir to combine. Bring back to a simmer, then cover tightly and cook over the lowest possible heat for 15 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes before fluffing with a fork and serving.

attrs.issue: Rice is sticking to the bottom of the pan

content.text: Reduce the heat further and check that the lid is tightly sealed. A layer of stuck rice at the very base is called socarrat in some traditions and is considered a good thing. Scrape and mix it through when serving.
Add 100 ml more hot stock, cover again and cook for another 5 minutes. Different rice varieties absorb stock at different rates.
The onions must be deeply browned before the spices go in. Pale onions give a flat result. Take your time on that step.

Pilau reached the Kenyan coast with Arab and Indian traders more than a thousand years ago. It took root in the Swahili kitchen and spread inland. Today it is served at weddings and celebrations across the country. The Mombasa version is famous for its richness and heavy spice. Every family has a slightly different spice ratio.
